rows.stem:
In the experimental setup given below, it is observed that on passing the gas produced in the reaction in the solution ‘X’ the solution ‘X’ first turns milky and then colourless.

The option that justifies the above stated observation is that ‘X’ is aqueous calcium hydroxide and

options.label: A
options.text: it turns milky due to carbon dioxide gas liberated in the reaction and after sometime it becomes colourless due to formation of calcium carbonate.

options.label: B
options.text: it turns milky due to formation of calcium carbonate and on passing excess of carbon dioxide it becomes colourless due to formation of calcium hydrogen carbonate which is soluble in water.

options.label: C
options.text: it turns milky due to passing of carbon dioxide through it. It turns colourless as on further passing carbon dioxide, sodium hydrogen carbonate is formed which is soluble in water.

options.label: D
options.text: the carbon dioxide liberated during the reaction turns lime water milky due to formation of calcium hydrogen carbonate and after some time it turns colourless due to formation of calcium carbonate which is soluble in water.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the reacting substances (dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium carbonate in a test tube, a delivery tube leading into a second test tube holding solution X) are named only in the drawing. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
Dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium carbonate to give carbon dioxide:

\(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 + 2HCl \rightarrow 2NaCl + H_2O + CO_2}\)

Passed into lime water, carbon dioxide forms insoluble calcium carbonate, which turns the solution milky:

\(\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2 + CO_2 \rightarrow CaCO_3 + H_2O}\)

With excess carbon dioxide the calcium carbonate changes to calcium hydrogen carbonate, which is soluble, so the solution becomes colourless again:

\(\mathrm{CaCO_3 + H_2O + CO_2 \rightarrow Ca(HCO_3)_2}\)

This is option (B) it turns milky due to formation of calcium carbonate and on passing excess of carbon dioxide it becomes colourless due to formation of calcium hydrogen carbonate which is soluble in water.

rows.stem: The emission of brown fumes in the given experimental set-up is due to

options.label: A
options.text: thermal decomposition of lead nitrate which produces brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide.

options.label: B
options.text: thermal decomposition of lead nitrate which produces brown fumes of lead oxide.

options.label: C
options.text: oxidation of lead nitrate forming lead oxide and nitrogen dioxide.

options.label: D
options.text: oxidation of lead nitrate forming lead oxide and oxygen.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the set-up (a test tube labelled lead nitrate held over a burner, with brown fumes labelled at its mouth) exists only in the drawing; the stem says only 'the given experimental set-up'. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
On heating, lead nitrate decomposes into lead oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. The brown fumes are nitrogen dioxide; lead oxide is a solid left in the tube.

\(\mathrm{2Pb(NO_3)_2(s) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2PbO(s) + 4NO_2(g) + O_2(g)}\)

This is option (A) thermal decomposition of lead nitrate which produces brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide.

rows.stem:
\(\mathrm{MnO_2} + x\,\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MnCl_2} + \mathrm{y\,H_2O} + \mathrm{z\,Cl_2}\)

In order to balance the above chemical equation, the values of \(x\), y and z respectively are :
rows.solution:
\(\mathrm{MnO_2 + 4HCl \rightarrow MnCl_2 + 2H_2O + Cl_2}\)

Check: Mn 1 = 1; O 2 = 2; H 4 = 4; Cl 4 on the left, and \(2 + 2 = 4\) on the right.

So x, y and z are 4, 2, 1, which is option (C) 4, 2, 1.

rows.stem:
The table below has information regarding pH and the nature (acidic/basic) of four different solutions. Which one of the options in the table is correct ?

| Option | Solution | Colour of pH paper | Approximate pH value | Nature of solution |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | Lemon juice | Orange | 3 | Basic |
| (b) | Milk of magnesia | Blue | 10 | Basic |
| (c) | Gastric juice | Red | 6 | Acidic |
| (d) | Pure water | Yellow | 7 | Neutral |

options.label: A
options.text: Lemon juice; Orange; 3; Basic

options.label: B
options.text: Milk of magnesia; Blue; 10; Basic

options.label: C
options.text: Gastric juice; Red; 6; Acidic

options.label: D
options.text: Pure water; Yellow; 7; Neutral

rows.solution:
Milk of magnesia is a mild base: its pH is about 10 and it turns pH paper blue. The other rows are wrong: lemon juice (pH about 3) is acidic, not basic; gastric juice is strongly acidic with a pH of about 1 to 2, not 6; and pure water (pH 7) turns pH paper green, not yellow.

This is option (B) Milk of magnesia; Blue; 10; Basic.

rows.stem: A metal ‘X’ is used in thermite process. When X is burnt in air it gives an amphoteric oxide ‘Y’. ‘X’ and ‘Y’ are respectively :

options.label: A
options.text: Fe and \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\)

options.label: B
options.text: Al and \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)

options.label: C
options.text: Fe and \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}\)

options.label: D
options.text: Al and \(\mathrm{Al_3O_4}\)

rows.solution:
Aluminium is used in the thermite process, where it reduces iron(III) oxide to molten iron:

\(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 2Al \rightarrow Al_2O_3 + 2Fe}\) + heat

Burnt in air, aluminium forms aluminium oxide, which reacts with both acids and bases and so is amphoteric:

\(\mathrm{4Al + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Al_2O_3}\)

This is option (B) Al and \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\).

rows.subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
rows.stem: Select washing soda from the following :

options.label: A
options.text: \(\mathrm{NaHCO_3}\)

options.label: B
options.text: \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3.5H_2O}\)

options.label: C
options.text: \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3.10H_2O}\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(\mathrm{NaOH}\)

rows.solution:
Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, with ten molecules of water of crystallisation. (\(\mathrm{NaHCO_3}\) is baking soda and NaOH is caustic soda.)

This is option (C) \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3.10H_2O}\).

rows.stem: Consider the structures of the three cyclic carbon compounds A, B and C given below and select the correct option from the following :

options.label: A
options.text: A and C are isomers of hexane and B is benzene.

options.label: B
options.text: A is an isomer of hexane, B is benzene and C is an isomer of hexene.

options.label: C
options.text: A is a saturated cyclic hydrocarbon and B and C are unsaturated cyclic hydrocarbons.

options.label: D
options.text: A is cyclohexane and B and C are the isomers of benzene.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the three compounds A, B and C are given only as drawn six-carbon ring structures with every C and H atom shown; the number and position of double bonds in each ring is what the options test and is withheld here. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
In A every carbon is joined to the next by a single bond and carries two hydrogens: it is cyclohexane, \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}}\), a saturated cyclic hydrocarbon. B has three alternating double bonds in the ring: it is benzene, \(\mathrm{C_6H_6}\). C has two double bonds in the ring (\(\mathrm{C_6H_8}\)).

B and C both contain carbon-carbon double bonds, so they are unsaturated. A is not an isomer of hexane (\(\mathrm{C_6H_{14}}\)), and C is not an isomer of benzene, since its molecular formula is different.

So A is saturated while B and C are unsaturated cyclic hydrocarbons. This is option (C).

rows.stem: An organism which breaks down the food material outside the body and then absorbs it is

options.label: A
options.text: a plant parasite, Cuscuta

options.label: B
options.text: an animal parasite, Tapeworm

options.label: C
options.text: a bacteria, Rhizobium

options.label: D
options.text: a fungi, Rhizopus

rows.solution:
*Rhizopus* (bread mould) is a saprophytic fungus. It releases digestive enzymes on the food outside its body, breaks it down into simple substances and then absorbs them. *Cuscuta* and tapeworm absorb food already made or digested by their host, and *Rhizobium* lives in the root nodules of legumes.

This is option (D) a fungi, *Rhizopus*.

rows.stem: Consider the following statements about small intestine and select the one which is NOT correct :

options.label: A
options.text: The length of the small intestine in animals differs as it depends on the type of food they eat.

options.label: B
options.text: The small intestine is the site of complete digestion of food.

options.label: C
options.text: The small intestine receives secretions from liver and pancreas.

options.label: D
options.text: The villi of the small intestine absorb water from the unabsorbed food before it gets removed from the body via the anus.

rows.solution:
The small intestine is the site of complete digestion; it receives bile from the liver and pancreatic juice from the pancreas; and its length depends on the diet (longer in herbivores, which digest cellulose). Water is absorbed from the unabsorbed food by the wall of the large intestine, not by the villi of the small intestine, whose villi absorb digested food.

The statement that is not correct is option (D) The villi of the small intestine absorb water from the unabsorbed food before it gets removed from the body via the anus.

rows.stem: The statement that correctly describes the characteristic(s) of a gene is :

options.label: A
options.text: In individuals of a given species, a specific gene is located on a particular chromosome.

options.label: B
options.text: A gene is not the information source for making proteins in the cell.

options.label: C
options.text: Each chromosome has only one gene located all along its length.

options.label: D
options.text: All the inherited traits in human beings are not controlled by genes.

rows.solution:
Genes are sections of DNA on the chromosomes. In a given species a particular gene always lies at a particular place on a particular chromosome. The other statements are false: a gene is the information source for making a protein, each chromosome carries many genes along its length, and inherited traits are controlled by genes.

This is option (A) In individuals of a given species, a specific gene is located on a particular chromosome.

rows.stem: Select from the following the correct statement about tropic movement in plants :

options.label: A
options.text: It is due to stimulus of touch and temperature.

options.label: B
options.text: It does not depend upon the direction of stimulus received.

options.label: C
options.text: It is observed only in roots and not in stems.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a growth related movement.

rows.solution:
A tropic movement is a directional growth movement: a part of the plant grows towards or away from a stimulus such as light, gravity, water or chemicals. Its direction depends on the direction of the stimulus, and it is seen in both roots and shoots.

This is option (D) It is a growth related movement.

rows.stem: Select the INCORRECT match (between the plant and its vegetative part) from the following :

options.label: A
options.text: Bryophyllum, leaf

options.label: B
options.text: Potato, stem

options.label: C
options.text: Money-plant, stem

options.label: D
options.text: Rose, root

rows.solution:
*Bryophyllum* produces new plants from buds on the margins of its leaves; potato and money-plant are propagated from their stems. Rose is propagated by stem cuttings, not by its roots.

So the incorrect match is option (D) Rose, root.

rows.stem: If four identical resistors, of resistance 8 ohm, are first connected in series so as to give an effective resistance \(\mathrm{R_s}\), and then connected in parallel so as to give an effective resistance \(\mathrm{R_p}\), then the ratio \(\dfrac{\mathrm{R_s}}{\mathrm{R_p}}\) is
rows.solution:
In series, \(R_s = 4 \times 8 = 32\,\Omega\).

In parallel, \(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{4}{8}\), so \(R_p = 2\,\Omega\).

\(\dfrac{R_s}{R_p} = \dfrac{32}{2} = 16\), which is option (D) 16.

rows.stem: In domestic electric circuits the wiring with 15 A current rating is for the electric devices which have

options.label: A
options.text: higher power ratings such as geyser.

options.label: B
options.text: lower power ratings such as fan.

options.label: C
options.text: metallic bodies and low power ratings.

options.label: D
options.text: non-metallic bodies and low power ratings.

rows.solution:
Domestic circuits have two lines: a 15 A line for appliances with higher power ratings, such as geysers, heaters and air coolers, and a 5 A line for bulbs, fans and other low-power devices.

This is option (A) higher power ratings such as geyser.

rows.stem: In the following diagram, the position of the needle is shown on the scale of a voltmeter. The least count of the voltmeter and the reading shown by it respectively are :

options.label: A
options.text: 0.15 V and 1.6 V

options.label: B
options.text: 0.05 V and 1.6 V

options.label: C
options.text: 0.15 V and 1.8 V

options.label: D
options.text: 0.05 V and 1.8 V

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the dial of a voltmeter (V) with a semicircular scale marked 0, 1.5 and 3 and a needle; the number of divisions and the needle position decide both the least count and the reading, and are withheld here. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
The scale runs from 0 to 3 V and is divided into 20 small divisions (with a longer mark every 5 divisions), so the least count is \(\dfrac{3}{20} = 0{\cdot}15\) V.

The needle stands 2 divisions beyond the 1.5 V mark, so the reading is \(1{\cdot}5 + 2 \times 0{\cdot}15 = 1{\cdot}8\) V.

This is option (C) 0.15 V and 1.8 V.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Current-carrying Conductor
rows.stem: The resultant magnetic field at point ‘P’ situated midway between two parallel wires (placed horizontally) each carrying a steady current I is

options.label: A
options.text: in the same direction as the current in the wires.

options.label: B
options.text: in the vertically upward direction.

options.label: C
options.text: zero

options.label: D
options.text: in the vertically downward direction.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - two horizontal parallel wires, AB above and CD below, with the point P marked midway between them; each wire carries an arrow giving the direction of its current, which decides the answer and is withheld here. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
Both wires carry the same current I in the same direction (A to B and C to D), and P is equidistant from them, so the two fields at P are equal in size. By the right-hand thumb rule, the upper wire AB gives a field at P (below it) directed into the plane of the paper, and the lower wire CD gives a field at P (above it) directed out of the plane. The two fields cancel.

This is option (C) zero.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The colour of aqueous solution of copper sulphate turns colourless when a piece of lead is added to it.

**Reason (R) :** Lead is more reactive than copper, and hence displaces copper from its salt solution.
rows.context:
Q. Nos. 17 to 20 are Assertion – Reason based questions.

These consist of two statements – Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Answer these questions selecting the appropriate option given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: C
options.text: (A) is true, but (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: (A) is false, but (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Lead is above copper in the reactivity series, so it displaces copper from copper sulphate solution:

\(\mathrm{Pb(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow PbSO_4(s) + Cu(s)}\)

The blue copper ions are removed and lead sulphate is colourless (and insoluble), so the blue solution turns colourless. The Assertion is true. The Reason is true and is the correct explanation, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Genes inherited from the parents decide the sex of a child.

**Reason (R) :** X chromosome in a male child is inherited from his father.
rows.context:
Q. Nos. 17 to 20 are Assertion – Reason based questions.

These consist of two statements – Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Answer these questions selecting the appropriate option given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: C
options.text: (A) is true, but (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: (A) is false, but (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The sex of a child is decided by the sex chromosomes inherited from the parents: a child who inherits an X chromosome from the father is a girl, and one who inherits a Y chromosome is a boy. So the Assertion is true.

A male child (XY) inherits his X chromosome from his mother and his Y chromosome from his father, so the Reason is false.

The Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Blood clotting prevents excessive loss of blood.

**Reason (R) :** Blood clotting is due to blood plasma and white blood cells present in the blood.
rows.context:
Q. Nos. 17 to 20 are Assertion – Reason based questions.

These consist of two statements – Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Answer these questions selecting the appropriate option given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: C
options.text: (A) is true, but (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: (A) is false, but (R) is true.

rows.solution:
When a blood vessel is injured, a clot forms and plugs the leak, so blood clotting prevents excessive loss of blood. The Assertion is true.

Clotting is brought about by the platelets in the blood (together with clotting proteins of the plasma). White blood cells fight infection and do not cause clotting, so the Reason is false.

The Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Current-carrying Conductor
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The strength of the magnetic field produced at the centre of a current carrying circular coil increases on increasing the number of turns in it.

**Reason (R) :** The current in each circular turn has the same direction and the magnetic field due to each turn then just adds up.
rows.context:
Q. Nos. 17 to 20 are Assertion – Reason based questions.

These consist of two statements – Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Answer these questions selecting the appropriate option given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: C
options.text: (A) is true, but (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: (A) is false, but (R) is true.

rows.solution:
In a circular coil the current in every turn flows in the same direction, so the field due to each turn at the centre is in the same direction and the fields add up. A coil of n turns therefore gives a field n times that of a single turn. The Assertion is true, and the Reason is true and explains the Assertion.

This is option (A).

rows.subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
rows.stem:
(i) A compound ‘X’ which is prepared from gypsum has the property of hardening when mixed with proper quantity of water.

Identify ‘X’ and write its chemical formula.

(ii) State the difference in chemical composition between baking soda and baking powder.
rows.solution:
(i) X is Plaster of Paris (calcium sulphate hemihydrate), \(\mathrm{CaSO_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}H_2O}\). It is made by heating gypsum at 373 K:

\(\mathrm{CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{373 K}} CaSO_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}H_2O + 1\frac{1}{2}H_2O}\)

Mixed with water, it changes back to gypsum and sets as a hard solid mass.

(ii) Baking soda is a single compound, sodium hydrogen carbonate, \(\mathrm{NaHCO_3}\). Baking powder is a mixture of baking soda and a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid.

rows.stem:
Write balanced chemical equation for the reaction that occurs when :

(i) blue coloured copper sulphate crystals are heated and

(ii) Sodium hydrogen carbonate is heated during cooking.
rows.solution:
(i) On heating, the blue crystals lose their water of crystallisation and become white anhydrous copper sulphate:

\(\mathrm{CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} CuSO_4 + 5H_2O}\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{2NaHCO_3 \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} Na_2CO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}\)

rows.stem:
(a) Write the role of insulin in regulating blood sugar levels in human body. Mention the disease caused due to it.

(b) How is the timing and the amount of release of insulin in the blood regulated ?
rows.solution:
(a) Insulin, secreted by the pancreas, lowers the blood sugar level by helping the cells take up glucose. If too little insulin is secreted, the blood sugar level rises and causes diabetes.

(b) By a feedback mechanism. When the sugar level in the blood rises, it is detected by the cells of the pancreas, which respond by producing more insulin. As the blood sugar level falls, insulin secretion is reduced.

rows.stem:
Name the type of blood (oxygenated / deoxygenated) transported by each of the following mentioning the path (i.e. from one organ (which place) to another (which place)).

(i) Vena cava

(ii) Pulmonary artery
rows.solution:
(i) The vena cava carries deoxygenated blood from the different parts of the body to the heart (the right atrium).

(ii) The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart (the right ventricle) to the lungs.

rows.stem:
With the help of a schematic flow chart, show the breakdown of glucose in a cell to provide energy –

(i) in the presence of oxygen

(ii) in lack of oxygen
rows.solution:
Glucose is first broken down to pyruvate in the cytoplasm in both cases.

(i) In the presence of oxygen:

\(\text{Glucose} \xrightarrow{\text{in cytoplasm}} \text{Pyruvate} \xrightarrow[\text{in mitochondria}]{\text{presence of oxygen}} \mathrm{CO_2} + \text{water} + \text{energy}\)

(ii) In lack of oxygen (in human muscle cells):

\(\text{Glucose} \xrightarrow{\text{in cytoplasm}} \text{Pyruvate} \xrightarrow[\text{in muscle cells}]{\text{lack of oxygen}} \text{Lactic acid} + \text{energy}\)

(In yeast, the pyruvate is instead converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide.)

rows.stem: Name the part of the human excretory system where nephrons are found. Write the structure and function of nephrons.
rows.solution:
Nephrons are found in the kidneys.

Structure: each nephron begins with a cluster of thin-walled blood capillaries, the glomerulus, held in a cup-shaped structure called Bowman's capsule. The capsule leads into a long tubular part, which ends in a collecting duct.

Diagram: draw the glomerulus inside Bowman's capsule, the branch of the renal artery bringing blood to it and the branch of the renal vein taking blood away, the coiled tubular part surrounded by capillaries, and the collecting duct. Label each part.

Function (any one): it filters nitrogenous wastes from the blood to form urine; it reabsorbs useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, salts and water from the filtrate; it regulates the amount of water in the body (osmoregulation).

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem:
A narrow beam XY of white light is passing through a glass prism ABC as shown in the diagram :

Trace it on your answer sheet and show the path of the emergent beam as observed on the screen PQ.

Name the phenomenon observed and state its cause.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the student must trace the printed figure: a triangular glass prism ABC with a narrow beam from X striking face AB at Y, and a vertical screen PQ to the right of the prism. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
Diagram: trace the prism ABC. The beam XY of white light enters face AB at Y and, inside the prism, splits into its seven colours, each bent through a different angle. The colours leave from the opposite face and spread out to form a band on the screen PQ: red, bent the least, at the top (towards P), and violet, bent the most, at the bottom (towards Q), in the order red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Draw arrows on the rays.

The phenomenon is the dispersion of white light.

Cause: the different colours of light bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through the prism, because they have different wavelengths and the glass has a slightly different refractive index for each.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.subtopic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
rows.stem:
It is observed that the power of an eye to see nearby objects as well as far off objects diminishes with age.

(i) Give reason for the above statement.

(ii) Name the defect that is likely to arise in the eyes in such a condition.

(iii) Draw a labelled ray diagram to show the type of corrective lens used for restoring the vision of such an eye.
rows.solution:
(i) With age the ciliary muscles gradually weaken and the eye lens loses its flexibility, so the eye cannot change its focal length enough.

(ii) Presbyopia. When both near and distant vision are affected, the person suffers from presbyopia together with myopia.

(iii) Such an eye is corrected by a bifocal lens. Diagram: draw a spectacle lens divided into two parts. The upper part is a concave lens, for distant vision, and the lower part is a convex lens, for near vision. Label both parts.

rows.stem: How do harmful chemicals get accumulated progressively at each trophic level in a food chain ?
rows.solution:
Pesticides and other chemicals sprayed on crops are washed down into the soil and the water bodies. From there they are absorbed by plants along with water and minerals, and enter the food chain when the plants are eaten by animals.

These chemicals are not degradable, so they are not broken down or excreted. They accumulate in each organism, and since each organism eats many organisms of the level below, their concentration increases progressively at each successive trophic level. This is called biological magnification, and organisms at the top of the chain, such as human beings, have the highest concentration.

rows.stem:
(a) Identify the reducing agent in the following reactions :

(i) \(\mathrm{4NH_3 + 5O_2 \rightarrow 4NO + 6H_2O}\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{H_2O + F_2 \rightarrow HF + HOF}\)

(iii) \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \rightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2}\)

(iv) \(\mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O}\)

(b) Define a redox reaction in terms of gain or loss of oxygen.
rows.solution:
(a) The reducing agent is the substance that is oxidised: it gains oxygen or loses hydrogen.

(i) \(\mathrm{NH_3}\): it gains oxygen to form NO (and loses its hydrogen to oxygen).

(ii) \(\mathrm{H_2O}\): it loses hydrogen to fluorine, which gains hydrogen and is reduced. (No oxygen is gained or lost by either reactant, so the gain-or-loss-of-oxygen definition alone cannot decide this part; the marking scheme awards it to everyone who attempts it.)

(iii) CO: it gains oxygen to form \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), while \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) loses oxygen.

(iv) \(\mathrm{H_2}\): it gains oxygen to form water.

(b) A redox reaction is one in which one reactant gains oxygen (is oxidised) while another reactant loses oxygen (is reduced), both at the same time.

rows.stem:
(a) Suggest one remedial measure each to counteract the change in pH in human beings in following cases :

(i) Production of too much acid in stomach during indigestion

(ii) Stung by a honey bee / nettle leaves

(b) Fresh milk has a pH of 6. When it changes into curd will its pH increase or decrease ? Why ?
rows.solution:
(a) (i) Take an antacid, a mild base such as milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide) or baking soda, which neutralises the excess acid in the stomach.

(ii) The sting injects methanoic acid. Rub a mild base such as baking soda solution on the area to neutralise it. For a nettle sting, rubbing the leaf of the dock plant, which often grows beside the nettle, gives relief.

(b) The pH decreases. When milk sets into curd, lactic acid is formed, so curd is more acidic than milk.

rows.stem:
(i) State the role of ATP in cellular respiration.

(ii) What ensures sufficient exchange of gases in plants ?

(iii) State the conditions on which the direction of diffusion of gases in plant depend upon.
rows.solution:
(i) The energy released during cellular respiration is used to make ATP, the energy currency of the cell. ATP is broken down to give a fixed amount of energy, which drives the energy-requiring (endothermic) reactions in the cell.

(ii) Gases are exchanged through the stomata in the leaves and through the surface of the leaves, stems and roots. Each cell is close to the air, so the gases diffuse in and out easily.

(iii) The direction of diffusion depends on the environmental conditions and on the requirements of the plant. At night, when there is no photosynthesis, carbon dioxide is given out and oxygen taken in; during the day, carbon dioxide made in respiration is used in photosynthesis, so oxygen is given out.

rows.stem:
(i) What is the internal energy reserve in plants and animals ?

(ii) How desert plants perform photosynthesis if their stomata remain closed during the day ?
rows.solution:
(i) Plants store energy as starch; animals store it as glycogen.

(ii) Desert plants open their stomata at night and take up carbon dioxide, which they store as an intermediate compound (an acid). During the day, with the stomata closed, this compound is acted upon by the energy absorbed by the chlorophyll, releasing carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

rows.stem:
(a) Complete the following ray diagram to show the formation of image :

(b) Mention the nature, position and size of the image formed in this case.

(c) State the sign of the image distance in this case using the Cartesian sign convention.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the ray diagram to be completed is given only as a drawing: object AB standing on the principal axis in front of a curved mirror with pole P, Ray 1 from A parallel to the axis and Ray 2 from A meeting the mirror and continued as a dashed line towards C, with points R and C marked on the axis. Which kind of mirror it is (shown only by its curvature and hatching) decides parts (b) and (c) and is withheld here. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
(a) The mirror bulges towards the object and C lies behind it, so it is a convex mirror. On the paper's figure the point midway between P and C is labelled R; it is the principal focus, which the marking scheme's diagram marks F.

Ray 1, parallel to the principal axis, is reflected so that it appears to come from the focus F: draw the reflected ray going back to the left and produce it backwards (dotted) to F behind the mirror. Ray 2, directed towards C, falls normally on the mirror and is reflected back along its own path. The dotted extensions of the two reflected rays meet behind the mirror at A'. Draw A'B' perpendicular to the axis: A'B' is the image.

(b) The image is virtual and erect, it is formed behind the mirror between P and F, and it is diminished.

(c) The image is behind the mirror, on the side opposite to the object, so the image distance is positive.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :

(a) Danger signals installed at airports and at the top of tall buildings are of red colour.

(b) The sky appears dark to the passengers flying at very high altitudes.

(c) The path of a beam of light passing through a colloidal solution is visible.
rows.solution:
(a) Red light has the longest wavelength and is scattered the least by fog or smoke. It therefore travels farthest and can be seen easily from a large distance.

(b) At very high altitudes there is hardly any atmosphere, so there are almost no particles to scatter sunlight. With no scattering the sky appears dark.

(c) The particles of a colloid are big enough to scatter light, so the beam is scattered by them and its path becomes visible (the Tyndall effect).

rows.stem:
(i) State the rule used to find the force acting on a current carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.

(ii) Given below are three diagrams showing entry of an electron in a magnetic field. Identify the case in which the force will be (1) maximum and (2) minimum respectively. Give reason for your answer.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - part (ii) rests on three printed panels (i), (ii) and (iii), each showing parallel magnetic field lines with arrows and a path labelled Electron; the angle each electron path makes with the field is the quantity under test and is withheld here. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
(i) Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the middle finger in the direction of the current, the thumb points in the direction of motion of the conductor, that is, of the force on it.

(ii) (1) The force is maximum in diagram (i), because the electron moves at right angles to the magnetic field.

(2) The force is minimum (zero) in diagram (iii), because the electron moves along, parallel to, the magnetic field.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Solenoid
rows.stem:
(i) Draw the pattern of magnetic field lines of

(1) a current carrying solenoid

(2) a bar magnet

(ii) List two distinguishing features between the two fields.
rows.solution:
(i) (1) Draw a solenoid connected to a cell and a key. Inside it the field lines are parallel straight lines along its axis; outside they curve round from one end to the other. Mark the ends S and N, with arrows going out of the N end and into the S end outside.

(2) Draw a bar magnet with poles N and S. The field lines leave the north pole, curve round outside the magnet and enter the south pole, and are closest together near the poles. Draw arrows on the lines.

(ii) Any two:

1. The strength of the field of a solenoid can be changed by changing the current; that of a bar magnet cannot be changed.

2. The direction of the field of a solenoid can be reversed by reversing the current; that of a bar magnet cannot be changed.

3. The field of a solenoid is temporary (it lasts only while the current flows); that of a bar magnet is permanent.

rows.stem:
(i) Why does a kitchen garden called an artificial ecosystem while a forest is considered to be a natural ecosystem ?

(ii) While designing an artificial ecosystem at home, write any two things to be kept in mind to convert it into a self-sustaining system. Give reason to justify your answer.
rows.solution:
(i) A kitchen garden is made and maintained by human beings, so it is an artificial (man-made) ecosystem and is not self-sustaining. A forest is maintained by nature without human intervention and sustains itself, so it is a natural ecosystem.

(ii) Taking an aquarium at home as the example:

1. Provide oxygen continuously, for instance through an air pump, because the animals need it for respiration.

2. Add aquatic plants along with the animals, because the plants (the producers) make food that serves the animals, and give out oxygen in sunlight.

(Any other correct example with a justification is equally acceptable.)

rows.stem:
(i) Construct a food chain of four trophic levels comprising the following :

Hawk, snake, plants, rat.

(ii) 20,000 J of energy was transferred by the producers to the organism of second trophic level. Calculate the amount of energy that will be transferred by organisms of the third trophic level to the organisms of the fourth trophic level.
rows.solution:
(i) Plants \(\rightarrow\) Rat \(\rightarrow\) Snake \(\rightarrow\) Hawk

(ii) By the 10% law, only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next.

The second trophic level (rat) receives 20,000 J. The energy passed from the second to the third level is \(\dfrac{10}{100} \times 20000 = 2000\) J, and the energy passed from the third level (snake) to the fourth level (hawk) is \(\dfrac{10}{100} \times 2000 = 200\) J.

rows.stem:
A saturated organic compound ‘A’ belongs to the homologous series of alcohols.

On heating ‘A’ with concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K, it forms an unsaturated compound ‘B’ with molecular mass 28 u.

The compound ‘B’ on addition of one mole of hydrogen in the presence of Nickel, changes to a saturated hydrocarbon ‘C’.

(i) Identify A, B and C.

(ii) Write the chemical equations showing the conversion of A into B.

(iii) What happens when compound C undergoes combustion ?

(iv) State one industrial application of hydrogenation reaction.

(v) Name the products formed when compound A reacts with sodium.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: its combustion equation for (iii), \(\mathrm{C_2H_6 + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 3H_2O}\), is not balanced (two O atoms on the left, seven on the right); balanced, it is as written below.]

(i) B is an unsaturated compound of molecular mass 28 u, so it is ethene, \(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\) (\(2 \times 12 + 4 \times 1 = 28\)). So A is ethanol, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\), and C is ethane, \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH_3}\).

(ii) Hot concentrated sulphuric acid removes water from ethanol:

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow{\text{conc. } H_2SO_4,\ 443\,K} CH_2{=}CH_2 + H_2O}\)

(iii) Ethane burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of heat (and light):

\(\mathrm{2C_2H_6 + 7O_2 \rightarrow 4CO_2 + 6H_2O}\) + heat

(iv) Hydrogenation is used in industry to convert vegetable oils into vegetable ghee (fats), using a nickel catalyst.

(v) Sodium ethoxide and hydrogen:

\(\mathrm{2CH_3CH_2OH + 2Na \rightarrow 2CH_3CH_2ONa + H_2}\)

rows.stem:
(i) With the help of diagram, show the formation of micelles, when soap is applied on oily dirt.

(ii) Take two test tubes X and Y with 10 mL of hard water in each.

In test tube ‘X’, add few drops of soap solution and in test tube ‘Y’ add a few drops of detergent solution. Shake both the test tubes for the same period.

(1) In which test tube the formation of foam will be more ? Why ?

(2) In which test tube is a curdy solid formed ? Why ?
rows.solution:
(i) A soap molecule has an ionic end (\(\mathrm{-COO^-Na^+}\)), which is attracted to water, and a long hydrocarbon tail, which is attracted to oil. When soap is applied to oily dirt, the tails of many soap molecules dissolve in the oil droplet while the ionic heads stay in the water.

Diagram: draw an oil droplet at the centre with many soap molecules arranged radially around it, each with its hydrocarbon tail pointing into the droplet and its ionic head (with \(\mathrm{Na^+}\)) pointing outwards into the water. This cluster is a micelle. Label the oil droplet and the ionic heads.

(ii) (1) More foam forms in test tube Y. Detergents are effective in hard water: they do not form insoluble substances with the calcium and magnesium ions, so they lather well.

(2) A curdy solid forms in test tube X. Soap reacts with the calcium and magnesium salts in hard water to form an insoluble precipitate, called scum.

rows.stem:
(a) Name the parts of a bisexual flower that are not directly involved in reproduction.

(b) Differentiate between self pollination and cross pollination. List any two significance of pollination.

(c) What is the fate of ovules and ovary after fertilization in a flower ?
rows.solution:
(a) The sepals (calyx) and the petals (corolla).

(b) Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower, or of another flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma of a flower on a different plant (of the same species).

Significance of pollination (any two): it is necessary for seed formation; it leads to fertilisation; it stimulates the development of fruits; cross-pollination brings about genetic variation.

(c) After fertilisation the ovule develops into the seed, and the ovary develops into the fruit.

rows.stem:
(a) An electric iron consumes energy at a rate of 880 W when heating is at the maximum rate and 330 W when the heating is at the minimum. If the source voltage is 220 V, calculate the current and resistance in each case.

(b) What is heating effect of electric current ?

(c) Find an expression for the amount of heat produced when a current passes through a resistor for some time.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: for the minimum setting it prints \(R = \dfrac{220}{115}\); the current there is \(1{\cdot}5\) A, so \(R = \dfrac{220}{1{\cdot}5} = 146{\cdot}7\,\Omega\), which is the value it gives (as 146.6).]

(a) At the maximum rate, \(P = 880\) W and \(V = 220\) V:

\(I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{880}{220} = 4\) A, and \(R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{220}{4} = 55\,\Omega\).

At the minimum rate, \(P = 330\) W and \(V = 220\) V:

\(I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{330}{220} = 1{\cdot}5\) A, and \(R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{220}{1{\cdot}5} \approx 146{\cdot}7\,\Omega\).

(Check: \(R = \dfrac{V^2}{P} = \dfrac{48400}{330} \approx 146{\cdot}7\,\Omega\).)

(b) When an electric current passes through a resistor, part of the electrical energy supplied by the source is dissipated in it and appears as heat. This is the heating effect of electric current.

(c) Let a current I flow through a resistor R for a time t, with a potential difference V across it. The charge that flows is \(Q = It\), and the work done in moving it through the potential difference V is

\(W = VQ = VIt\).

This energy is dissipated in the resistor as heat, so \(H = VIt\). Since \(V = IR\),

\(H = I^2Rt\) (Joule's law of heating).

rows.stem: What happens when copper is heated in air ? (Give the equation of the reaction involved).
rows.context: Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides. Metal oxides are generally basic in nature. But some metal oxides show both basic as well as acidic behaviour. Different metals show different reactivities towards oxygen. Some react vigorously while some do not react at all.
rows.solution:
Copper does not burn, but when heated in air it combines with oxygen and becomes coated with black copper(II) oxide:

\(\mathrm{2Cu + O_2 \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2CuO}\)

rows.stem: Why are some metal oxides categorized as amphoteric ? Give one example.
rows.context: Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides. Metal oxides are generally basic in nature. But some metal oxides show both basic as well as acidic behaviour. Different metals show different reactivities towards oxygen. Some react vigorously while some do not react at all.
rows.solution: Some metal oxides react with both acids and bases to produce salt and water, so they show both basic and acidic behaviour; such oxides are called amphoteric. Example: aluminium oxide, \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) (or zinc oxide, ZnO).

rows.stem:
Complete the following equations :

(i) \(\mathrm{Na_2O_{(s)} + H_2O_{(l)} \rightarrow}\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 2\,NaOH \rightarrow}\)
rows.context: Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides. Metal oxides are generally basic in nature. But some metal oxides show both basic as well as acidic behaviour. Different metals show different reactivities towards oxygen. Some react vigorously while some do not react at all.
rows.solution:
(i) \(\mathrm{Na_2O(s) + H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq)}\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH \rightarrow 2NaAlO_2 + H_2O}\) (sodium aluminate and water)

rows.subtopic: Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
rows.stem:
On burning Sulphur in oxygen a colourless gas is produced.

(i) Write chemical equation for the reaction.

(ii) Name the gas formed.

(iii) State the nature of the gas.

(iv) What will be the action of this on a dry litmus paper ?
rows.context: Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides. Metal oxides are generally basic in nature. But some metal oxides show both basic as well as acidic behaviour. Different metals show different reactivities towards oxygen. Some react vigorously while some do not react at all.
rows.solution:
(i) \(\mathrm{S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2}\)

(ii) Sulphur dioxide.

(iii) It is acidic (a non-metallic oxide).

(iv) No change. Sulphur dioxide shows its acidic nature only when dissolved in water (\(\mathrm{SO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_3}\), sulphurous acid), so it has no action on dry litmus paper; it turns moist blue litmus red.

rows.stem: Write any two pairs of contrasting characteristics of pea plant used by Mendel other than those mentioned above.
rows.context: In order to trace the inheritance of traits Mendel crossed pea plants having one contrasting character or a pair of contrasting characters. When he crossed pea plants having round and yellow seeds with pea plants having wrinkled and green seeds, he observed that no plants with wrinkled and green seeds were obtained in the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation. When the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation pea plants were cross-bred by self-pollination, the \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation had seeds with different combinations of shape and colour also.
rows.solution: Any two: tall and dwarf plants (height of the plant); violet (purple) and white flowers (colour of the flower); axial and terminal flowers (position of the flower); green and yellow pods (colour of the pod); inflated and constricted pods (shape of the pod).

rows.stem: Differentiate between dominant and recessive traits.
rows.context: In order to trace the inheritance of traits Mendel crossed pea plants having one contrasting character or a pair of contrasting characters. When he crossed pea plants having round and yellow seeds with pea plants having wrinkled and green seeds, he observed that no plants with wrinkled and green seeds were obtained in the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation. When the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation pea plants were cross-bred by self-pollination, the \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation had seeds with different combinations of shape and colour also.
rows.solution: A dominant trait is expressed even when only one copy of the gene for it is present (it shows itself in the presence of the contrasting trait). A recessive trait is suppressed by the dominant one and is expressed only when both copies of the gene are for the recessive trait.

rows.stem: State the ratio of the combinations observed in the seeds of \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation (in the above case). What do you interpret from this result ?
rows.context: In order to trace the inheritance of traits Mendel crossed pea plants having one contrasting character or a pair of contrasting characters. When he crossed pea plants having round and yellow seeds with pea plants having wrinkled and green seeds, he observed that no plants with wrinkled and green seeds were obtained in the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation. When the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation pea plants were cross-bred by self-pollination, the \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation had seeds with different combinations of shape and colour also.
rows.solution:
The \(\mathrm{F_2}\) seeds are round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green \(= 9 : 3 : 3 : 1\).

Interpretation: round green and wrinkled yellow are new combinations, so the traits for seed shape and seed colour are inherited independently of each other.

rows.stem:
Given below is a cross between a pure violet flowered pea plant (V) and a pure white flowered pea plant (v). Diagrammatically explain what type of progeny is obtained in \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation and \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation :

Pure violet flowered plant \(\times\) Pure white flowered plant.

(V V) (v v)
rows.context: In order to trace the inheritance of traits Mendel crossed pea plants having one contrasting character or a pair of contrasting characters. When he crossed pea plants having round and yellow seeds with pea plants having wrinkled and green seeds, he observed that no plants with wrinkled and green seeds were obtained in the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation. When the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation pea plants were cross-bred by self-pollination, the \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation had seeds with different combinations of shape and colour also.
rows.solution:
Parents: pure violet (VV) \(\times\) pure white (vv). The gametes are V and v, so every \(\mathrm{F_1}\) plant is Vv. Violet is dominant, so all the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) plants have violet flowers.

\(\mathrm{F_1}\) plants are self-pollinated: Vv \(\times\) Vv. Each produces gametes V and v in equal numbers.

| Gametes | V | v |
|---|---|---|
| V | VV (violet) | Vv (violet) |
| v | Vv (violet) | vv (white) |

The \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation has VV : Vv : vv \(= 1 : 2 : 1\), that is, 3 violet-flowered plants to 1 white-flowered plant.

rows.stem: List two applications of concave mirror.
rows.context: Hold a concave mirror in your hand and direct its reflecting surface towards the sun. Direct the light reflected by the mirror on to a white card-board held close to the mirror. Move the card-board back and forth gradually until you find a bright, sharp spot of light on the board. This spot of light is the image of the sun on the sheet of paper; which is also termed as “Principal Focus” of the concave mirror.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the passage's ray diagram: rays parallel to the principal axis reflected by a concave mirror (pole O) and meeting at F, with 'Principal Focus' and 'Principal axis' labelled; the passage text carries everything the sub-parts need. Page idx 30.
rows.solution: Any two: torches, searchlights and vehicle headlights (to get a powerful parallel beam of light); shaving mirrors and dentists' mirrors (to see an enlarged image); solar furnaces (to concentrate sunlight).

rows.stem: If the distance between the mirror and the principal focus is 15 cm, find the radius of curvature of the mirror.
rows.context: Hold a concave mirror in your hand and direct its reflecting surface towards the sun. Direct the light reflected by the mirror on to a white card-board held close to the mirror. Move the card-board back and forth gradually until you find a bright, sharp spot of light on the board. This spot of light is the image of the sun on the sheet of paper; which is also termed as “Principal Focus” of the concave mirror.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the passage's ray diagram: rays parallel to the principal axis reflected by a concave mirror (pole O) and meeting at F, with 'Principal Focus' and 'Principal axis' labelled; the passage text carries everything the sub-parts need. Page idx 30.
rows.solution: The focal length is \(f = 15\) cm, and \(R = 2f = 2 \times 15 = 30\) cm.

rows.stem: Draw a ray diagram to show the type of image formed when an object is placed between pole and focus of a concave mirror.
rows.context: Hold a concave mirror in your hand and direct its reflecting surface towards the sun. Direct the light reflected by the mirror on to a white card-board held close to the mirror. Move the card-board back and forth gradually until you find a bright, sharp spot of light on the board. This spot of light is the image of the sun on the sheet of paper; which is also termed as “Principal Focus” of the concave mirror.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the passage's ray diagram: rays parallel to the principal axis reflected by a concave mirror (pole O) and meeting at F, with 'Principal Focus' and 'Principal axis' labelled; the passage text carries everything the sub-parts need. Page idx 30.
rows.solution:
With the object AB between the pole P and the focus F of a concave mirror, draw two rays from A. A ray parallel to the principal axis is reflected through F. A ray directed along the line from C through A falls normally on the mirror and is reflected back along its own path through C. The reflected rays diverge; produce them backwards (dotted) behind the mirror, where they meet at A'. Draw A'B' perpendicular to the axis.

The image A'B' is formed behind the mirror and is virtual, erect and enlarged.

Draw arrows on all the rays.

rows.stem:
An object 10 cm in size is placed at 100 cm in front of a concave mirror. If its image is formed at the same point where the object is located, find :

(i) focal length of the mirror, and

(ii) magnification of the image formed with sign as per Cartesian sign convention.
rows.context: Hold a concave mirror in your hand and direct its reflecting surface towards the sun. Direct the light reflected by the mirror on to a white card-board held close to the mirror. Move the card-board back and forth gradually until you find a bright, sharp spot of light on the board. This spot of light is the image of the sun on the sheet of paper; which is also termed as “Principal Focus” of the concave mirror.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the passage's ray diagram: rays parallel to the principal axis reflected by a concave mirror (pole O) and meeting at F, with 'Principal Focus' and 'Principal axis' labelled; the passage text carries everything the sub-parts need. Page idx 30.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: two lines of its working drop the minus sign of u, printing \(\dfrac{1}{100} - \dfrac{1}{100}\) and \(m = \dfrac{-(-100)}{100}\); with \(u = -100\) cm they are \(-\dfrac{1}{100} - \dfrac{1}{100}\) and \(\dfrac{-(-100)}{-100}\). Its answers, \(f = -50\) cm and \(m = -1\), are correct.]

The image is formed where the object is, so \(u = -100\) cm and \(v = -100\) cm.

(i) By the mirror formula,

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{100} - \dfrac{1}{100} = -\dfrac{2}{100}\), so \(f = -50\) cm.

(The image coincides with the object only when the object is at the centre of curvature, so \(R = 100\) cm and \(f = \dfrac{R}{2} = 50\) cm, negative for a concave mirror.)

(ii) \(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-100}{-100} = -1\).

The image is real, inverted and the same size as the object (\(h' = -10\) cm).
